name: Gabonese Poulet Nyembwe
description: Poulet nyembwe, chicken in a real palm-nut sauce, is Gabon's national dish, its name literally meaning 'palm oil' in the Myene language - real versions traditionally use smoked chicken, which gives the dish a deeper, more distinctive flavor than fresh chicken alone; this version uses fresh chicken as the more practical substitute. Real palm nut cream isn't a distinct item here, so peanut butter stands in, the same widely recognized substitute used across neighboring Congo and Angola.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, garlic, and ginger, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and jalapeño, then add to the pot.
Simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.

Simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is very tender.

name: Gabonese Odika (Wild Mango Seed Sauce)
description: Odika, sometimes called 'African chocolate', is a real Gabonese sauce made from roasted, ground wild mango seeds - real odika isn't a distinct item here, so peanut butter stands in for a similarly rich, nutty base, though it honestly lacks odika's real, distinctive chocolate-like depth.

name: Gabonese Fufu
description: Fufu, cassava or yam pounded into a smooth, stretchy dough, is a genuine Gabonese staple, traditionally torn by hand to scoop up sauce.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.

name: Gabonese Mustard Chicken
description: Gabonese-style mustard chicken, marinated with lemon, garlic, and chili before roasting, is a beloved everyday Gabonese dish, real technique letting the marinade sit so the mustard's tang genuinely penetrates the meat.
steps_detailed: Mix the mustard, lemon juice, garlic, and jalapeño, then rub over the chicken and marinate at least 20 minutes.
Roast at 400F (200C) for 30-35 minutes, or grill, until golden and cooked through.

name: Gabonese Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Gabonese side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in a little oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.
